title: What do you actually mean by “AI trading”?
author: CapDue4077
selftext:
Most AI trading bots I see here follow a strategy their owner defined (RSI, MA crossovers, breakouts…), and the AI writes the code or executes the signals. Nothing wrong with that, but to me that’s algo trading with an AI helper.

My bot (built with Claude, I’m not a programmer) works the other way round: there’s no strategy in the code. An LLM gets market data, a few candidates, news and its open positions about 11 times a day, and decides on its own whether to go long, go short, tighten a stop, close, or do nothing. It has to explain every decision, including the reasons against it.

The code only enforces guardrails the AI can’t override: a broker-side stop on every position (it can only be tightened), plus limits on leverage, position size, and daily loss. My test for every rule is whether it prevents something dangerous or tells the AI what to trade. Only the first kind stays in.

The result is pretty boring. Most runs end with “hold, no new trade.” I started on a demo account recently, and the second week (balanced risk profile) was profitable. That proves nothing, it’s just an experiment, but it’s fun to read its reasoning.

So: what does “AI trading” mean to you? An AI that executes your strategy, or one that makes the decisions itself?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the guardrail test is good, stop something dangerous vs tell it what to trade. the catch with the LLM-decides version is you can't backtest it honestly, the model has already read the news for every date you'd replay. on the US stock side, I made Quantradin so an agent like yours can run a fake money account before a real one, free. quantradin.com  how are you judging it so far?

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body:
Thanks, and good point. That’s exactly why I don’t backtest it at all. It only runs forward on a broker demo account, so every decision is made without knowing what happens next. I’m already set up there, so I’ll stick with that for now.

How I judge it so far: mostly on behavior, not P&L. Does it follow the rules, are its reasons coherent, does it handle stops and exits the way it planned, and does it run stable without me touching it? I also log a simple buy-and-hold reference (world ETF + Bitcoin) next to it. But with a handful of trades per week, I’d need months before the returns say anything.

comments.author: Infamous_Food_3766
comments.body: i'm using ai for research and building the bot, with explicit trading rules still being tested. for your setup, are u saving the exact prompt, model version and inputs for every decision? would be useful if a model update changes its behaviour halfway through the experiment.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: Yes, mostly. For every decision I store the full input the model saw, its complete answer, and the exact model version that actually responded, as reported by the API. The system prompt isn’t stored per decision, but it’s version-controlled and every change is logged with a timestamp, so I can tell which version was active for any run. And you’re right that a model update mid-experiment would be a confounder. I’d treat it like any other change and mark it in the log.

replies.author: Infamous_Food_3766
replies.body: makes sense. i'd stick the prompt version or commit hash directly in each decision record too, just to avoid matching it back by timestamp later. if u change the model, keeping the before/after results separate would make the experiment much easier to follow.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: Good call, that’s exactly what I just added to my to-do list after your first comment: a fingerprint of the exact system prompt in every decision record, plus the full text of each new version. The model version is already stored per decision, so before/after a model change can be split cleanly. Thanks, this was genuinely useful.

replies.author: Infamous_Food_3766
replies.body: nice, glad it helped. would be interesting to see what u learn after a few months of forward testing.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: I’ll definitely post an update once there are a few months of data, good or bad.

replies.author: Infamous_Food_3766
replies.body: sounds good, the rough or flat months would be just as useful to see as the good ones. looking forward to the update.

comments.author: teckel
comments.body: Because AI alone is a terrible method of stock picking.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: You might well be right, and I’m not expecting it to beat the market. There’s no proof LLMs have an edge at picking stocks. For me it’s more of an experiment: can an AI make its own trading decisions, explain them, and stay within hard risk limits, without me feeding it a strategy? If it ends up losing to buy and hold, that’s a valid result too.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: counting a loss to buy and hold as a real result is a good way to set it up. one behaviour check I'd add: does it size the same after three losers as after three winners. that's where LLM-run accounts tend to drift without anyone telling them to.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: Good point. Right now it can’t really drift that way, because it only sees its open positions, not its past wins and losses. But I’m planning to give it a trade journal so it can learn from closed trades, and that’s exactly where your check becomes relevant. I’ll compare position sizing after losing and winning streaks before and after that change.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
the journal is where that check earns its keep. log two sizes per entry, the one it picked and the one your rules allow, and drift shows up as a gap you can chart.

if you ever want a second forward run beside the demo, I built Quantradin (quantradin.com), where an agent trades the same rules on live prices with fake money, no charge.

replies.author: teckel
replies.body: The problem is that AI will hallucinate to find you an answer (a stock to buy). I prefer to use AI as just part of an automated deterministic agent. 100% automated doing all real-money buys and sales.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: I tried to design around it: doing nothing is explicitly a valid answer, and that’s what it picks most of the time. In the second week it opened nothing in 54 of 60 runs. It doesn’t look anything up itself. Prices and indicators come from the code, and every order is checked against live prices and hard limits before it goes out. So the deterministic part is still there, it just sits around the AI instead of inside the strategy.

comments.author: vishr
comments.body:
I’d keep AI-assisted research as a third bucket. The distinction for me is who chooses the trading action.

I build Monk.trade and use Claude to turn research criteria into scans and charts. With Oct 23 data, I screened US common stocks above their 200-day average and up over 20 sessions, with at least $20M average daily dollar volume over the prior 20 sessions. That found 686 confirmed matches. Requiring volume at least 1.5 times its prior 20-session average left 68; 277 remained undecided because of insufficient history or stale data.

That narrows a research list; it doesn’t establish a trading edge. Your setup gives the model discretion over trading decisions. Mine leaves those decisions with the person.

[Research example: scan, refinement and chart](https://imgur.com/a/cBFTG5D)

Research only. Not investment advice.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: I like that framing: the real question is who chooses the trading action. Three buckets makes sense to me: AI-assisted research (you decide), AI executing your rules (the rules decide), and AI as the decision-maker (the model decides, within hard limits). Mine is the third one. Funny enough, my screener is the opposite of yours: half liquidity, half random, so I don’t sneak a momentum filter in before the model even gets to decide.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I'd say both count, but they're different things to test. Your split is clear, and putting the limits in code where the model can't override them is the part I'd copy. Since the model decides on its own, the check I'd add is to run the same inputs a few times and see if it makes the same call, because a decision you can't repeat is hard to judge. Compare it against a simple baseline too, like doing nothing, over a longer period, since one profitable week on a demo says little. Cymetica lets you connect your own AI agent and run it in paper mode first, which is a similar way to build that record.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: Repeatability is a great check, and it’s easy for me because I store the full input of every decision, so I can replay old runs later and see how often it makes the same call. For baselines I track buy and hold (world ETF + Bitcoin), and doing nothing is simply the starting balance. Agreed that one week says nothing, it’ll take months.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Storing the full input of every decision so you can replay it is a strong setup, and tracking buy and hold as the baseline keeps the comparison honest. Giving it months before judging is the right call.

comments.author: drguid
comments.body:
I do algorithmic trading with AI of the machine learning variety. Basically I feed it backtest data of the winners and losers and it spits out which properties can help identify the winners.

Does it work? It's looking good. It's particularly good at avoiding trades with high drawdowns and low CAGR.

Also it's very efficient (mine uses a CPU) and once the model is built it can score hundreds of stocks a minute.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: Mine is almost the opposite: an LLM that reads news and argues its case. It’s slow and expensive, and it can’t be backtested honestly because the model already knows the past. How do you keep it from overfitting to the backtest?

comments.author: Technical-Athlete-9
comments.body: Same concept for me except that AI gets the lists of candidates and holdings to monitor news and filings. I’m considering some ML systems, but I’m not convinced of my testing methods for that yet. I don’t let LLMs do entries, but I might get there after better evals for my agents.

replies.author: CapDue4077
replies.body: A demo account is basically my eval for that last step: I let the LLM do entries with play money and hard limits, so I can see how it behaves before trusting it with anything real.
